title: Chapter 53 — The Gam
paragraphs: The stated reason why Ahab did not go aboard the whaler we had spoken was this: the wind and sea threatened storms. But even had this not been the case, he would probably not have boarded her anyway — judging by his later conduct on similar occasions — if by hailing her he had gotten a negative answer to the question he asked. For, as it eventually turned out, he had no interest in socializing even for five minutes with any stranger captain, unless that captain could contribute some of the information he so obsessively sought. But all this might remain unexplained without some account of what a Gam is among whalemen.

If two strangers crossing the Pine Barrens in New York State, or the equally desolate Salisbury Plain in England, happen to encounter each other in such unwelcoming wilds, those two, for the life of them, cannot well avoid a mutual greeting — and stopping for a moment to exchange news, and perhaps sitting down for a while to rest together. How much more natural, then, that upon the limitless Pine Barrens and Salisbury Plains of the sea, two whaling vessels spotting each other at the ends of the earth — off lonely Fanning's Island, or the faraway King's Mills — how much more natural that under such circumstances these ships should not only exchange salutes, but take more involved steps toward socializing. And especially since it is an unavoidable thing that most whalers are away from home for at least three or four years at a stretch.

For the long-absent ship, the outward-bound vessel perhaps has letters on board. At any rate, she will be sure to share some newspapers of a date a year or two more recent than the last one in her blurred and thumb-worn files. And in return for that courtesy, the outward-bound ship would receive the latest whaling intelligence from the cruising-ground to which she may be headed — a thing of the utmost importance. And to some degree, all this holds true of whaling vessels crossing each other's paths on the cruising-ground itself, even though both are equally long absent from home. For one may have received recent mail from a friendly passing vessel, while the other has received none at all.

Nor would difference of country make any essential difference — at least so long as both parties speak the same language, as is the case with Americans and English. Though to be sure, given the small number of English whalers, such meetings do not happen very often. And when they do, there tends to be a sort of shyness between them. For your Englishman is rather reserved, and your Yankee does not appreciate that quality in anyone but himself. Besides, the English whalers sometimes display a kind of big-city superiority over the American whalers, regarding the long, lean Nantucketer with his antiquated equipment as a sort of poor rustic cousin.

So we see that of all ships separately sailing the sea, whalers have the most reason to be sociable — and they are. Whereas some merchant ships, crossing each other's path in the mid-Atlantic, will often pass without so much as a single word of acknowledgment, cutting each other on the high seas like a pair of dandies on Broadway. And all the while silently criticizing each other's rigging. As for warships, when they happen to meet at sea, they first go through such a long string of silly bowing and scraping, such a dipping of flags, that it is almost as ridiculous as two aristocrats meeting on a staircase, each insisting the other go first.

But look at the godly, honest, unpretentious, hospitable, sociable, free-and-easy whaler! What does the whaler do when she meets another whaler in any sort of decent weather? She has a Gam — a thing so utterly unknown to all other ships that they have never even heard the name. And if by chance they should hear of it, they only grin and repeat mocking stuff about "spouters" and "blubber-boilers" and similar pretty expressions. Why all merchant-seamen, and also all pirates and men-of-war sailors and slave-ship sailors, harbor such scornful feelings toward whale-ships is something that requires a separate chapter for its explanation. But for now, let us proceed.

But what is a Gam? You might wear out your index finger running up and down the columns of dictionaries and never find the word. Dr. Johnson never achieved that level of learning. Noah Webster's dictionary does not contain it. Nevertheless, this same expressive word has for many years been in constant use among some fifteen thousand true-born Americans. Certainly, it needs a definition and should be added to the dictionary. With that aim in mind, let me offer a learned definition.

GAM. Noun — A social meeting of two (or more) whale-ships, generally on a cruising-ground; when, after exchanging hails, they exchange visits by boats' crews: the two captains remaining, for the time, on board of one ship, and the two chief mates on the other.

There is another small detail about gamming that must not be forgotten here. All professions have their own little quirks of practice. So does the whale fishery. In a pirate ship, man-of-war, or slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern on a comfortable, sometimes cushioned seat, and often steers himself with a pretty little decorated tiller, hung with gay cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no stern seat, no sofa of any kind, and no tiller at all. Grand times indeed, if whaling captains were wheeled about the ocean in that fashion! In a whale-boat, the captain goes to visit another ship in the same way every other man does — practically sitting on the boat's bottom. And often, the most athletic captain will choose the bow oar for the trip. In his own boat, the visiting captain is given no special seat. He goes and comes an equal among equals — at least in this regard.
